claims.new_fact_bis: Ang himsog nga mga tanom adunay itom-berde nga mga dahon ug lig-on nga tul-id nga mga tangkay, nga nagpakita nga nakakuha sila ug igong kahayag sa adlaw, tubig, ug hangin.
claims.reason: The adversarial rejection rests on a miscounted statistic. Its '19 corpus bodies attest sanga = stem' is a co-occurrence artifact: it counted cards whose ENGLISH merely contains the string 'stem' somewhere, including cards where 'sanga' in fact renders 'branch'. The corpus's own controlled minimal pairs — cards where both words appear in one sentence — never once use sanga for stem. English says 'sturdy upright stems'; the Cebuano says 'sturdy upright branches', which sets a false criterion for plant health (the seedlings, herbs and vegetable plants a grade-5 child actually observes have no branches at all, yet are healthy). tangkay is the card's own intended word — it is listed in `terms`. Minimal change: sanga -> tangkay, nothing else touched; emphasis span 'itom-berde nga mga dahon' preserved verbatim.
claims.evidence: ceb_usage --bis sanga: 283 bodies, 30 titles, glossed 'branch' throughout; 222 bodies pair sanga with English 'branch'. ceb_usage --en stems: top Cebuano renderings are punoan 58 and tangkay 32 — sanga does not appear in the table. Corpus minimal pairs, decisive: ffct-05710 'What is a node on a plant stem? ... where a leaf or branch grows' -> 'Ang node sa TANGKAY sa tanom ... motubo ang dahon o SANGA'; ffct-13593 'the stem is above ground and holds up the leaves, branches, and flowers' -> 'ang PUNOAN naa sa ibabaw ... nagkupot og dahon, SANGA, ug bulak'; ffct-04814 'stems, roots, or branches' -> 'PUNOAN, gamot, o SANGA'; dcard-02474 'from the stem or twig' -> 'sa STEM o SANGA' (leaves 'stem' in English rather than use sanga). Of the 3 cards the adversarial cited, ffct-03708 ('cut plant stems' -> 'putlon ang sanga') and ffct-08580 ('a cut piece of its stem' -> 'giputol nga sanga') are cuttings/scions, which are branches in ordinary speech; ffct-02152 calls a potato tuber a 'sanga', itself a defect. Dictionary: binisaya.com/cebuano/sanga defines sanga as 'a division of a stem, or secondary stem arising from the main stem' — explicitly a branch, explicitly NOT the main stem. Wiktionary/kaikki: Cebuano tangkay = 'stem, stalk (of a plant), handle'. Corpus tangkay = 104 bodies, 28 titles (ffct-00926 'stems and leaves' -> 'tangkay ug dahon'; ffct-01442 'lower stem' -> 'ubos nga tangkay'; ffct-00871 'top of its stem' -> 'tumoy sa tangkay').

claims.new_fact_bis: Ang mga itom nga butang maayo nga mosuyop ug mopagawas sa radiation, samtang ang puti o sinaw nga butang mas mopabalik sa init ug magpabiling mas bugnaw ilalom sa adlaw.

That leaves 'mopalta' with exactly ONE independent body in 47,056 cards (and that one, ffct-38285, is itself a dubious rendering). Meanwhile the dictionary refutes the word outright: palta is the Spanish 'falta', meaning absent/lacking, with no bounce or reflect sense. So 'mas mopalta sa init' does not deliver 'reflect more heat' — it reads as 'lacks the heat more', which silently deletes the card's entire science point (the mechanism of reflection) and converts a cause into a restatement of the effect. mopabalik is attested in precisely this bounce-back sense with the identical verb form and identical 'sa X' frame. Minimal change: one verb; emphasis span 'itom' preserved. NOTE for the applier: title_bis 'Ang Itom Mosuyop, Ang Puti Mopalta' carries the same bad word and needs the same fix — it is out of scope for new_fact_bis.

Treat as unsourced.'). ceb_usage --bis mopalta: 2 bodies, one of which IS dcard-07176 itself, so 1 independent body. The adversarial's dcard-03213 actually reads 'ang kinaiya sa light nga MOTALBOG gikan sa sinaw nga butang' — no 'palta'. Corpus renderings of 'reflect' across 245 cards: salamin 48, nag-reflect 34, mobalik 27, plus motalbog/mosalpo — palta appears nowhere. On the 22 'reflect heat/sunlight' cards: ffct-23625 'aron IBALIK ang silaw sa kainit', ffct-27899 'ang light colors NAGBA-BALIK sa heat radiation', ffct-22685 'aron i-reflect PABALIK', ffct-19963 'ang puti nag-reflect sa sunlight'. mopabalik precedent, exact sense and exact frame: ffct-02746 'a mirror-like layer at the back that bounces light back out' -> 'nga MOPABALIK SA kahayag'; ffct-14264 'bounces its sound straight back' -> 'MOPABALIK SA tingog diretso'. Stem 'pabalik' = 150 bodies.

claims.new_fact_bis: Ang wick mao ang parte sa lampara nga mosuyop sa sugnod ug mogunit sa kalayo.
claims.reason: Both halves of the adversarial rejection fail against the corpus's own cards. (a) 'gasolina is the standard rendering of generic fuel (112 bodies)': the 112 is the count of the literal English word 'fuel' surviving untranslated in Cebuano bodies, not of gasolina. The real split is gasolina 87 vs sugnod 85 — essentially tied, not a house standard. And where the corpus needs precision it uses gasolina contrastively as GASOLINE, listed beside kerosene and diesel as a different substance. (b) 'a wick cannot absorb firewood': the corpus itself calls kerosene 'usa ka likido nga sugnod' — a liquid fuel — and the dictionary lists 'fuel' as a sense of sugnod, so the firewood objection is answered by the very corpus the adversarial appealed to. The defect is real and not merely stylistic: English says generic 'fuel', and telling a Filipino child that a lamp wick soaks up gasolina is both false (lamps burn gaas/kerosene) and unsafe, since gasoline in a lamp explodes. sugnod matches the English's generic 'fuel' exactly; 'gaas' (kerosene) would be the concrete alternative but narrows the English, so I kept the generic. Minimal change: one noun; emphasis span 'wick' preserved verbatim.
claims.evidence: ceb_usage --en fuel (366 cards): gasolina 87, sugnod 85 — the adversarial's '112' is the untranslated English token 'fuel' (112), not gasolina. Corpus uses gasolina contrastively as gasoline: ffct-15415 'We also burn gas (LPG), gasoline, and kerosene' -> 'gas (LPG), GASOLINA, ug KEROSENE' (distinct items); ffct-31908 'separate it into gasoline, kerosene, diesel' -> 'mahimong GASOLINA, kerosene, diesel'; ffct-15990 likewise. Decisive against the firewood objection: ffct-18348 'Kerosene, or gaas, is a LIQUID FUEL from petroleum' -> 'Ang kerosene o gaas usa ka likido nga SUGNOD gikan sa petrolyo'. sugnod also renders body fuel in ffct-02205 ('fuel that keeps them going' -> 'mao kini ang SUGNOD sa lawas'). Dictionary: binisaya.com/cebuano/sugnod lists two senses — 'firewood (n.) wood used for fuel' AND 'fuel (n.) a substance that can be consumed to produce energy'. Corpus sugnod = 95 bodies total. Real-lamp precedent: ffct-28384 'Oil climbs up the wick and burns' -> 'Mosaka ang GAAS sa PABILO ug masunog' (the corpus's own word for wick is 'pabilo', but 'wick' is an emphasis span here so it must stay).

claims.new_fact_bis:
Nganong mag-awit ang lalaki nga kuliglig?

Aron danihon ang baye nga kuliglig isip kapikas.
claims.reason: This is exactly the case the task warns about: a machine-translated corpus wrong in bulk, with frequency mistaken for attestation. 'kagang' is a CRAB in both Wolff and binisaya. A child reading only the Cebuano learns that a male crab sings to attract a female crab — a flat falsehood about the animal, provable from the card's own English ('a male cricket sing'). The adversarial's defence ('9 bodies, never once for crab') is self-defeating: all 8 kagang bodies are cricket cards and nothing else, which is the signature of one bulk mistranslation pass, not independent usage. Dictionary evidence beats corpus frequency. The card's own title_bis already says 'Awit sa KULIGLIG' and 'kuliglig' is the first entry in its `terms` list, so the body currently contradicts its own title; the repair also removes that internal inconsistency. Caveat recorded honestly: kuliglig is Tagalog-origin and this corpus also uses it for cicada (ffct-01016), and Cebuano-proper candidates exist (gangis, kuliklik, kulilig). Which insect word is best is a separate, smaller question for a native speaker; it does not licence leaving a crab in a cricket card. emphasis_bis is empty, nothing to preserve.
claims.evidence: Wolff, A Dictionary of Cebuano Visayan: 'kágang — a kind of small crab of muddy areas near the shore, with highly prized flesh'; kagangkagang = small land crab, inedible, venomous bite. binisaya.com/cebuano/kagang: 'crab (n.)', 'land crab (n.)'. Neither lists any insect sense. ceb_usage --bis kagang: 8 bodies, 0 titles, and every single one is a cricket card (ffct-00655, 01825, 01874, 03568, 03598, 03727, 04846, 11910) — a single contaminated cluster, not independent attestation. ceb_usage --en cricket (35 cards): kuliglig 28 vs kagang 11. ceb_usage --bis kuliglig: 38 bodies, 25 titles. The corpus's own naming card ffct-01368: 'Why is the cricket called kuliglig?' -> 'Nganong KULIGLIG ang tawag niini?'. Residual noted: binisaya has no entry for kuliglig; bohol.ph gives 'kuliklik'/'kulilig' for cricket; binisaya gives gangis = cicada (corpus: gangis 1 body).

claims.new_fact_bis: Ang kuliglig, apan, ug katydid managsoon diay — sakop sila sa usa ka grupo sa mga insekto nga maayong molukso!
claims.reason: Same confirmed defect as ffct-00655, and worse here because the card is explicitly about taxonomy: the English says crickets, grasshoppers and katydids are all related jumping insects, while the Cebuano says a CRAB is related to grasshoppers and katydids and belongs to a group of jumping insects. A crab is not an insect, so the Cebuano teaches a false classification — the exact thing the card exists to teach correctly. The adversarial's '8 independent bodies' are not independent: they are the same single mistranslation cluster, and dictionary evidence (Wolff: kagang = small crab) beats corpus frequency. Minimal change: kagang -> kuliglig only; emphasis span 'managsoon' preserved verbatim. Two residuals I deliberately did NOT touch, since the instruction is to change only what is wrong: 'apan' correctly means grasshopper here (attested), but it is also the everyday conjunction 'but', so 'Ang kuliglig, apan, ug katydid' stays ambiguous — a separate readability question, not a falsehood; and the Cebuano drops 'big' from 'one big group', which is trivial.
claims.evidence: Wolff: 'kágang — a kind of small crab'; binisaya.com/cebuano/kagang = 'crab', 'land crab'. ceb_usage --bis kagang: 8 bodies, all cricket cards, 0 titles. ceb_usage --en cricket: kuliglig 28 vs kagang 11 across 35 cards. claims.reason: Evidence genuinely cannot settle this one, and I would rather say so than manufacture a verdict. The question is narrow: does the Cebuano collocation 'panahon sa pagpanganak' idiomatically mean 'breeding season', or does it literally mean 'birthing season'? If literal, there is a real defect — a MALE pig does not give birth, and the mane is a courtship display grown before mating rather than during the females' birthing period, so the card would misplace the event in the animal's cycle. If idiomatic (as Filipino biology register arguably is, cf. 'panahon ng pag-aanak'), the old text is fine and the swap is pure word preference. A dictionary cannot adjudicate a collocation: it will gloss panganak as 'give birth' and pasanay as 'breed', neither of which answers whether the phrase as a whole has drifted to mean breeding season. Three things cut against repairing: the corpus is split on the IDENTICAL fact; the card's own `terms` list explicitly equates 'breeding season' with 'panahon ng pag-aanak' and 'pagpanganak', so the existing body matches its author's stated intent; and the adversarial's cited precedent is real, not fabricated. This is register/idiom — exactly the NEEDS-NATIVE category. A native speaker should be asked one question: reading 'Sa panahon sa pagpanganak' cold, do you hear 'breeding season' or 'birthing season'?
claims.evidence: Corpus split on 'breeding season' across 7 cards: 'panahon sa pagpanganak' in ffct-00845, ffct-05468, ffct-08175, ffct-08919, ffct-12567; 'panahon sa pagpasanay' in ffct-06981. Decisively split on the SAME fact — ffct-00845 'During breeding season, egrets grow long, beautiful plumes' -> 'Panahon sa PAGPANGANAK' vs ffct-06981 'Egrets grow beautiful long feathery plumes during the breeding season' -> 'kung panahon na sa PAGPASANAY'. So the adversarial's citation of ffct-00845 is accurate but non-probative: its twin says the opposite. pasanay is well attested in the breed/reproduce sense (29 bodies: ffct-02497 'where mosquitoes breed' -> 'magpasanay ang lamok'; ffct-03214 'breeding them in safe centers' -> 'pagpasanay kanila sa luwas nga mga sentro'; ffct-04424 'so fish can breed' -> 'makapasanay ang mga isda'), and pagpanganak = 25 bodies. Card's own terms: ['breeding season', 'panahon ng pag-aanak', 'pagpanganak'] — the author's own gloss endorses the existing wording.

claims.new_fact_bis:
Ngano nga mabulokon ang mga tabo sa pitcher plant?

Ang mga tabo kasagaran mabulokon nga morag bulak aron mas madani ang mga insekto.
claims.reason: The adversarial answered the wrong question. It is right that 'tabo' is the corpus's word for a pitcher-plant pitcher and right that the English ANSWER says just 'Pitchers' — but the defect is in the QUESTION, and the English question says 'pitcher plants' in full. The omission is therefore provable from the card's own English. It matters because 'tabo' standing alone is the household water dipper to any Filipino child: 5 of the 12 corpus bodies containing 'tabo' use it that way, including two handwashing cards and the Big Dipper. And the Cebuano side of this card never names the plant anywhere — title_bis is the bare Latin 'Nepenthes' — so a grade-5 reader gets 'Nepenthes / Why are the dippers colorful? The dippers are usually colorful like flowers so they attract insects', and the only concrete noun available to them means a bathroom scoop. The fix restores the subject the English carries and matches the corpus's own house pattern for this exact word. Also note the adversarial's framing that 'nothing was repaired — no word was replaced' treats a pure addition as a non-edit; restoring a dropped subject is a repair. Minimal change: three words added to the question only, answer untouched; emphasis span 'mabulokon' preserved verbatim.
claims.evidence: ceb_usage --bis tabo: 12 bodies. Pitcher-plant sense (7), and in nearly every one the plant is named in the same sentence, which is precisely the context this card lacks: ffct-02847 'Sa sulod sa TABO SA PITCHER PLANT'; ffct-03766 'Daghang NEPENTHES morag baging ... nga adunay nagbitay nga TABO'; ffct-09994 'Ang bitik sa PITCHER PLANT ... morag lawom nga TABO'; ffct-10073 'Unsaon pagdakop sa PITCHER PLANT sa insekto? ... sa sulod sa TABO'; ffct-13096 'Ang PITCHER PLANT naghimo og tam-is nga nektar sa ngabil sa TABO niini'. Dipper sense (5), unprompted: ffct-03819 'wash properly using a tabo or a bottle' -> 'gamit ang TABO'; ffct-13739 'A tabo and pail still work great' -> 'ang TABO ug balde'; ffct-33191 'seven bright stars shaped like a ladle' -> 'porma og TABO'; dcard-02852 'looks like a tabo with a handle'. Only one other card shares this bare-tabo omission (ffct-11205), so it is a defect pattern, not the house style. Card's English question verbatim: 'Why are pitcher plants so brightly colored?'

claims.new_fact_bis:
Ngano baho kaayo ang Rafflesia?

Tinuyo nga mobaho ang Rafflesia sama sa dunot nga karne aron makadani og mga langaw nga motabang sa polinasyon niini.
claims.reason: The adversarial is correct that the proposed text was byte-identical to the old text, which means no repair was ever attempted and nothing was vindicated — so I re-derived from scratch, and there IS a defect. English: 'flies that help POLLINATE it'. Cebuano: 'motabang sa PAGPAMULAK niini' = 'help it to BLOOM/FLOWER'. That is a false causal claim a child will take literally: flies do not make the Rafflesia open its flower, they carry pollen between flowers. It also destroys the card's science point, since pollination is the whole reason the stink evolved. The corpus proves this is a mistranslation rather than a house rendering: 'pamulak' is overwhelmingly bloom/flower/spring (it is even the word for the SEASON spring), and the corpus's own near-duplicate Rafflesia card states the fact correctly. Minimal change: one noun phrase, pagpamulak -> polinasyon, using the corpus's exact construction 'motabang sa polinasyon'. emphasis_bis is empty, so nothing to preserve.
claims.evidence: ceb_usage --bis pamulak: 18 bodies, dominantly bloom/flower/spring — ffct-09776 'it blooms in big clusters' -> 'ang PAMULAK sa kahoy sa mangga ... MAMULAK'; ffct-05751 'make mango trees flower' -> 'MAGPAMULAK sa mangga'; ffct-14710 'makes mango trees flower' -> 'MAKAPAMULAK sa mga punoan'; and 'TINGPAMULAK' = the season spring in ffct-34705, ffct-02470, ffct-34058, dcard-01472, dcard-09108. Only 2 bodies stretch it toward pollination (ffct-07113, ffct-12166) and both are loose paraphrases of the same shape. The corpus's real renderings across 122 'pollinat' cards: polinasyon 12, plus the nagpolinate/pagpollinate loan and 'nagdala sa polen'. Decisive sister card, same fact, done right — ffct-00264 'Why does the Rafflesia smell so bad? Its foul smell attracts flies, which carry pollen from one Rafflesia flower to another for pollination' -> 'Ang baho niini nag-akit sa mga langaw nga NAGDALA SA POLEN gikan sa usa ka bulak ngadto sa lain'. Exact construction precedent for the repair: ffct-00304 'help pollinate flowers' -> 'motabang sa POLINASYON sa mga bulak'; ffct-01309 'Pollination moves pollen from one flower to another' -> 'Ang POLINASYON mao ang pagbalhin sa polen'.

claims.reason: The adversarial cited two outliers; I scanned all 127 cards whose English says 'rough'. claims.new_fact_bis: Ang magnet mobira lang og puthaw sama sa lansang, pero ang static charge makabira og papel, buhok, o tubig! Lahi sila nga puwersa.

claims.new_fact_bis: Delikado ang mga matalas nga butang sama sa lansang ug kutsilyo tungod kay ang gamay nga tumoy nagpugos sa tanan nga puwersa sa gamay nga lugar, naghimo og dako nga presyon nga dali nga mosulod sa panit!

Here the stakes are higher: this is a safety card listing dangerous sharp objects, and 'matalas nga butang sama sa pako ug kutsilyo' pairs a knife with what the corpus calls a wing 272 times — the hazard named simply fails to land. Dictionary gives pako = wing/fern only and lansang = hardware nail. Single-word edit; emphasis span 'presyon' kept verbatim.
claims.evidence: binisaya.com/cebuano/pako: only 'Athyrium esculentum (n.) [utanon]; fern (n.)' and 'wing (n.)'. binisaya.com/cebuano/lansang: 'nail (hardware) … hammered into materials as a fastener'. Exact-word corpus scan: pako = 272 WING / 55 FERN / 6 nail across 349 bodies; hardware-nail cards lansang 38 vs pako 6. claims.new_fact_bis: Sa junkyard, mogamit ang crane og giant electromagnet aron alsahon ang tibuok awto, ug ibuhian kini sa pag-off sa current!
claims.reason: Both dictionaries make buhat = do/make/create/work with no lifting sense, while alsa is explicitly hoist/lift/raise. The adversarial's own star witness undoes it: ffct-28711 renders the same English verb twice, using 'pag-alsa' in the question and 'buhaton' in the answer — an internal MT slip, not a convention. Across all 389 English-'lift' cards the corpus uses alsa 113 times to buhat 31 (and most of those 31 are genuine 'do/make' uses). The false belief is direct: a child reads that the crane's electromagnet MAKES the whole car, which destroys the magnetic-lifting point the card exists to teach. Single-word edit; emphasis span 'giant electromagnet' kept verbatim.
claims.evidence: binisaya.com/cebuano/buhat: 'deed (n.); compose, create, make, moil, work (v.)' — no lift sense. binisaya.com/cebuano/alsa: 'hoist (v.) … lift (v.) — raise or haul up …; raise (v.) — raise from a lower to a higher position'. ffct-28711 EN 'lift heavy bamboo frames' → BIS 'Unsaon PAG-ALSA … aron BUHATON ang bug-at nga bamboo frames' (both in one card). Attested replacement: ffct-00154 'aron alsahon ug dad-on kini balik sa pugad' for EN 'to lift it and carry it back to the nest'; 'alsahon' = 18 bodies; ceb_usage --en lift table: pag-alsa 63, buhaton absent from the top 25.

claims.new_fact_bis: Naabtan ka sa gawas samtang may kidlat? Pagyuko og ubos, ipundok ang mga tiil, itago ang ulo sa tuhod. Ayaw paghigda! Mas gamay ang target nimo ug mas luwas ka.
claims.reason: The adversarial rejected the PROPOSED WORDING, not the defect — it objected that 'Yumuko' is a Tagalog import and that the edit bundled a second swap, and it helpfully supplied the correct Cebuano itself ('Pagyuko og ubos', ffct-30102). Dictionaries give lubo = lob/balloon/dehusk (the corpus uses it for a burn blister) and duha = two, so 'duhaon ang mga tiil' does not deliver 'feet together'. This is a lightning-safety card issuing an unparseable instruction. I adopt the adversarial's own preferred form and the corpus's verbatim rendering of the identical English clause, avoiding the Tagalog import it objected to. emphasis_bis is empty, so nothing to preserve.
claims.evidence: Twin card ffct-35122, same English clause 'crouch low with your feet together' → 'yukbo ka ug IPUNDOK ANG MGA TIIL aron dili ka dali ma-igo sa kidlat!'. ffct-30102 EN 'Crouch down low' → 'PAGYUKO OG UBOS'. Corpus counts: paglubo 1 (this card), duhaon 1 (this card), lubo 2 (ffct-05138/ffct-05872, both = burn blister), vs pagyuko 4, yukbo 5, moduko 9, ipundok 5. binisaya.com/cebuano/lubo: 'lob (v.); lobo — balloon, wolf, swell; dehusk (v.)' — no crouch. binisaya.com/cebuano/yuko: 'bent (adj.); stooped (adj.) … with bent back'. 'Yumuko' confirmed Tagalog-leaked: only ffct-24472/24473.

claims.new_fact_bis: Ang anvil kay usa ka bug-at, solidong metal nga gamit! Naghatag kini og gahi nga surface para sa pag-martilyo ug pag-hubog sa ubang init nga metal.
claims.reason: The adversarial defended only the pag-hubog half and expressly conceded the other ('even if hugot→gahi were warranted'), rejecting the proposal for being larger than the defect. So I repair only the conceded half and leave pag-hubog untouched, which answers its objection exactly. hugot = taut/tight, not hard: dictionary is unambiguous, and 4 of the 5 corpus cards whose English says 'hard surface' use gahi — this card is the lone outlier. An anvil's defining property is hardness, so 'hugot nga surface' ('a taut surface') fails to deliver the fact. Single-word edit. NOTE for the record: pag-hubog is left as-is per the adversarial, but it is not clean — both binisaya.com and pinoydictionary give hubog = drunk/groggy/intoxicated only, with no shape sense, and the corpus's own word for shaping is hulma/porma. That half is worth a native check separately.
claims.evidence: ceb_usage --en 'hard surface' = 5 cards; gahi in 4: ffct-24194 'nagkinahanglan og gahi nga ibabaw', ffct-24205 'gahi nga bongbong', ffct-25370 'gahi ug makinis nga mga ibabaw', ffct-37554 'gahi nga surface' (the exact replacement phrase, also ffct-39547). Only ffct-21030 uses hugot. binisaya.com/cebuano/hugot: 'intense; taut — pulled or drawn tight; tense; tight' — hard absent. binisaya.com/cebuano/gahi: 'hard; stiff; tough'. ceb_usage --bis hugot = 169 bodies, all 'tightly/firmly' (ffct-00624 'gamot nga hugot nga naggunit sa yuta'). Separately: --bis hubog = 4 bodies only; binisaya + cebuano.pinoydictionary both give hubog = 'drunk, groggy, intoxicated' only; ceb_usage --en shaping top terms: pagporma 8, gihulma 3, naghulma 3.

claims.reason: Dictionary and corpus genuinely disagree and neither settles it. Both dictionaries give halo as a NOUN = monitor lizard (plus a verb 'mingle'); the noun sense 'a mixture' is not in either, and sagol is dictionary-attested as both noun and verb. But the corpus really has adopted halo as a mixture-noun in 21 bodies concentrated in exactly this chemistry cluster, so the adversarial's attestation claim is broadly accurate (I verified 21, after stripping halo-halo the dessert, the solar halo, the lizard, and the Tagalog verb pag-halo from the 64 raw \bhalo\b hits). Crucially it fails the false-belief test: 'solid nga halo sama sa harina' is disambiguated by the flour context, so a child does not come away believing something untrue — the risk is that the technical term collides with the word for bayawak and fails to attach. That is a register/loanword judgement, and it is a 21-card systemic question, not a one-card repair; fixing this card alone would leave it inconsistent with its 20 siblings. A Cebuano speaker should rule on the cluster.
claims.evidence: binisaya.com/cebuano/halo: 'monitor lizard (n.)' and 'mingle (v.)' — no mixture noun. cebuano.pinoydictionary.com/word/halo: 'hello; lizard; mingle'. binisaya.com/cebuano/sagol: 'ingredient (n.); blend, mingle, mix (v.)'. Corpus: halo as mixture-noun = 21 bodies (ffct-18129, ffct-18157, ffct-18386, ffct-18424, ffct-18491, ffct-19735, ffct-19830, ffct-20239, ffct-20270, ffct-20507, ffct-20528, ffct-21006, ffct-21138, ffct-21210, ffct-32790, ffct-32796, ffct-33091, ffct-33196, ffct-34761 …); halo = lizard in ffct-00855/04887/06130/13022, = solar ring in ffct-25541/29844/29845/29846/32621/34277. Against that, ceb_usage --en mixture ranks sagol 136 in 516 cards, and the same cluster uses it: ffct-16903 'heterogeneous nga sagol', ffct-17287 'Ang sagol heterogeneous'.

claims.new_fact_bis:
Unsa ang aurora?

Ang aurora mao ang nagkidlap nga lunhaw o rosas nga kahayag sa langit duol sa mga polo sa Kalibutan! Maporma kini kung moigo ang gagmay nga tipik gikan sa adlaw sa hangin sa atmospera.
claims.reason: Overturning the adversarial on dictionary evidence, not opinion. fact_en says "Earth's poles"; the Cebuano says "poste sa Kalibutan", and two Cebuano dictionaries give poste ONLY as a physical upright post, with no pole sense at all — so the child reads "near Earth's posts". The adversarial's case was pure frequency inside a corpus that is itself machine-translated: the same corpus renders this exact concept with polo, and the very cards it cited carry "Polo" in their own titles while the body says "poste" (ffct-22203 title "Sama nga Polo", ffct-22439 title "Polo sa Magnet", ffct-28949 title "Aurora Polo") — a card contradicting itself is not a considered lexical choice, it is an MT artifact (English "pole" -> phonetic "poste"). Residual, stated honestly: binisaya lists polo only as polo shirt/the sport, so polo is not dictionary-verified for the geographic sense either; it qualifies under the corpus-attested arm of the REPAIR bar and is corroborated by human-written Philippine-language usage. Only the one word changed; emphasis_bis is empty.
claims.evidence: binisaya.com/cebuano/poste: sole sense "post ... a piece of timber or metal fixed firmly in an upright position" (lamppost, gatepost, goalpost) — no geographic/magnetic pole sense. cebuano.pinoydictionary.com/word/poste: "post", nothing else. ceb_usage.py --bis poste = 72 bodies, dominated by literal posts: ffct-01526 "suga sama sa bombilya o poste", ffct-02318 "coco lumber alang sa poste ug tabla sa balay", ffct-15069 "poste sa kuryente". ceb_usage.py --en "Earth's poles" = 6 cards, and 3 of them use polo/pole: ffct-29107 "Bugnaw ang mga polo sa Yuta", ffct-32136 "Dili duol sa mga polo sa Earth", ffct-09834 "gikan sa Amihanang Polo paingon sa Habagatang Polo". External human-written attestation for polo = geographic pole: bcl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habagatan_na_Polo "An Habagatan na Polo ... iyo an pinakahabagatan na punto sa Kinaban"; Filipino school text "Ang Polong Hilaga ... ang Polong Timog". A web search for "amihanang poste"/"habagatang poste" returns no real-world use for Earth's poles — only the binisaya entry for poste = post.

claims.new_fact_bis:
Makita ba nato ang aurora sa Pilipinas?

Kasagaran dili, kay duol ta sa ekwador! Mas sagad makita ang aurora sa mga dapit nga duol sa amihanan o habagatang polo sa Kalibutan.

Separately and NOT acted on here (title repairs are out of scope for this field): title_bis "Aurora sa Ekwador" = "Aurora at the Equator" actively contradicts title_en "Auroras Near the Poles" and the card's own point that we cannot see them here — that title should be queued for the c5a-title pass.

Corpus for the identical north/south-pole phrasing: ffct-09834 "gikan sa Amihanang Polo paingon sa Habagatang Polo ug balik matag tuig" (EN "from near the North Pole to near the South Pole"); ffct-29107 "Bugnaw ang mga polo sa Yuta" (EN "Earth's poles stay cold"). claims.new_fact_bis:
Ngano nga dili ka dapat motan-aw sa adlaw?

Ang pagtan-aw sa atong pinakaduol nga bituon makadaut permanente sa retina ug makapahinabo og partial nga pagkabuta!
claims.reason: The adversarial already conceded the mudunggo half (dunggo = snout / to dock or land, never "look at" — "mudunggo sa adlaw" reads "dock at the sun"), so a repair was owed regardless. I am also keeping the pagkabulag -> pagkabuta half, and I can beat the adversarial's evidence rather than merely disagree: binisaya's bulag entry has eighteen senses and every one is separation, with no blindness sense, and the Wolff-derived examples are all separation too. Decisively, inside THIS corpus pagkabulag means separation in science contexts more often than it means blindness — so leaving it makes the sentence read "causes partial separation", which is exactly the homonym collision the card cannot afford. buta is both the dictionary word and the corpus's dominant one. Both changes are single-word; emphasis_bis is empty.
claims.evidence: dunggo: ceb_usage.py --bis dunggo = 1 body, ffct-03354 "ang ilang nawong ug dunggo susama sa iro nga fox" (snout). bulag: binisaya.com/cebuano/bulag — "separate (adj.)", "apart (adv.)", "force, take, or pull apart", "divide into components", "discontinue an association or relation; go different ways"; no blindness sense. cebuano.pinoydictionary.com/word/bulag gives Wolff examples all meaning separate: "Adtu ku mubulag nimu sa iskina", "Nagbulag ang managtratu". Corpus, pagkabulag = 5 bodies and 2 are SEPARATION: ffct-17574 "Unsaon pagkabulag sa mga bahin sa chromatography" (EN "How does chromatography separate a mixture?") and dcard-00696 "nagpapaspas sa pagkabulag sa hydrogen peroxide" (EN "speeds up the breakdown"). Against that, buta is the corpus's blindness word: 22 bodies with bare buta (ffct-00041 "gipanganak nga buta" = born blind; ffct-02038 "mabasa sa mga buta ang braille") plus pagkabuta in 6 bodies (ffct-03279 "aron malikayan ang pagkabuta", EN "to prevent blindness"). The adversarial cited 3 pagkabulag hits and never checked a dictionary or the competing buta.

claims.new_fact_bis: Kung nagluto kung magsugod ang linog, palonga ang kalan kung maabot nga luwas, dayon duko, tago, ug kupot!
claims.reason: This is not an overturn — the adversarial rejected the proposal only because it was a byte-identical no-op, so the defect was never adjudicated. Re-deriving from the English: fact_en ends "drop, cover, and hold", and the Cebuano ends "duko, tago, ug kumot". kumot is not "hold" in Cebuano — the dictionary gives wring/crush/squeeze, and this corpus uses it for a throat spasm or (as a Tagalog leak) a blanket. So the third and most important step of a life-safety earthquake drill is lost: the child is told to drop, hide, and wring/crumple. kupot is dictionary-verified as "grip/hold" and is the corpus's normal word with 326 bodies. Deliberately left alone as clumsy-but-not-false: the doubled "Kung ... kung", and duko/tago for drop/cover.
claims.evidence: binisaya.com/cebuano/kumot: "wring (n.); crush (v.); squeeze (v.)" — no hold or grip sense. Corpus kumot = 6 bodies: ffct-06945 "sakit nga pagkumot sa tutunlan" (throat spasm), ffct-11156 "morag mokumot ang tiyan" (stomach clenching), ffct-23641 "Sama kini og kumot aron magpabilin nga init ang pagkaon" and ffct-28851 "sama sa dako nga dili makita nga kumot" (blanket — Tagalog sense), ffct-13451 (mat of duckweed), plus this card. binisaya.com/cebuano/kupot: "grip (v.); hold (v.)", synonyms kapot, kubot. Corpus kupot = 326 bodies, e.g. ffct-03549 "gigamit aron kuptan ug gunitan ang ilang biktima" (EN "used to grab and hold onto their prey"). The corpus's other three drop-cover-hold cards keep the English term — ffct-36141 "sa drop, cover, ug hold", ffct-36294 "mag-drop, mag-cover, ug mag-hold on", ffct-34918 quotes the drill name — so ffct-38479 is the only card that translates the drill, and it mistranslates the step that keeps the child under the table.

claims.new_fact_bis: Ang collapsible steering column gidisenyo aron mub-an sa frontal crash! Kini usa ka gamit nga nagpakunhod sa kadaot sa dughan sa driver.
claims.reason: Also not an overturn: the adversarial accepted that nagpaliti is a real, unattested defect (root palit = to buy, so the sentence says the device "causes the harm to buy") and rejected the earlier proposal only because it left the garbled genitive chain in place. This repair answers that objection instead of re-arguing it — nagpaliti becomes the dictionary-verified, heavily attested nagpakunhod, and the chain "kadaot sa manibela sa dughan sa driver" (readable as "harm of the chest's steering wheel") loses the "sa manibela" that fact_en never states, so the clause now says exactly what the English says: does less harm to the driver's chest. mub-an is left as-is because it is attested for "becomes shorter". emphasis_bis is empty.
claims.evidence: ceb_usage.py --bis paliti = 0 bodies, "NOT ATTESTED IN ANY CEBUANO BODY"; nagpaliti = 1 body, this card. binisaya.com/cebuano/kunhod: "abate (v.); diminish (v.); dwindle (v.); reduce (v.); subside (v.)". Corpus kunhod = 402 bodies, nagpakunhod = 37, including the same harm-reduction frame: ffct-07395 "nagpakunhod sa risgo sa pinsala sa kaunuran" (EN "lowers the risk of muscle injury"). mub-an kept on attestation: dcard-04746 "motaas ang projectile apan mub-an ang horizontal range" (EN "its horizontal range becomes shorter"), plus pamub-an/mapamub-an/kinamub-an across 24 bodies. fact_en is "This device does less harm to the driver's chest" — there is no steering-wheel-to-chest relation in it, which is why dropping "sa manibela" is a narrowing, not a rewrite.

claims.new_fact_bis: Ang mga butang magkalahi sa usag usa base sa mga physical property sama sa kagahi, pagkasinaw, ug pagka-stretchable, nga atong maobserbahan gamit ang atong mga igbalati.
claims.reason: Textbook attestation-bucket close, plus a second defect the gate did not flag. (1) The old word is not pagkasinaw but pagkakasaw, whose root kasaw means "splash" — the child reads "hardness, splashiness, and stretchability". pagkasinaw is a regular pagka- nominalisation of a dictionary-verified root, so its single corpus hit is rarity, not evidence against it — and that single hit is the very same physical-properties list. (2) fact_en says "observe with our senses" but the Cebuano says "gamit ang atong mga panan-aw" = using our eyesight. You cannot see hardness or stretchability, so on a card whose whole subject is observing with the senses the Cebuano teaches a false method; igbalati is the corpus's own, unambiguous word for senses. emphasis_bis span "physical property" is preserved verbatim.
claims.evidence: binisaya.com/cebuano/kasaw: "splash (v.)" and related splashing senses — nothing about shine. Corpus "kasaw" = 1 body: this card. binisaya.com/cebuano/sinaw: "brilliance (n.); glared (n.); luster (n.) — the visual property of something that shines with reflected light; shine (v.)". Corpus sinaw = 58 bodies (ffct-00295 "sinaw nga agi sa uhog" = shiny slime trail); pagkasinaw = 1 body, dcard-04618 "sama sa pagkagahi, pagka-flexible, o pagkasinaw" (EN "like being hard, flexible, or shiny") — the identical construction. panan-aw = 115 bodies, all vision (ffct-00084 "Mas talinis ang panan-aw sa agila" = eagle's eyesight). igbalati = 15 bodies, all "senses": ffct-04315 "Aduna kitay lima ka organ sa igbalati: ang mata, dalunggan, ilong, dila, ug panit" (EN "We have five sense organs"), ffct-00123 "mga mensahe gikan sa imong mga igbalati" (EN "messages from your senses").

claims.new_fact_bis: Ang tephra kay mga tipik nga volcanic debris nga kusganong gipagawas sa atmosphere panahon sa explosive eruptions, ug kini makaabot ug tinagpulo ka kilometro sa taas sa bulkan.
claims.reason: The hold is closable exactly as the bucket description predicts: binisaya does have tinagpulo, and the tag-/tinag- distributive series is productive in Cebuano, so one corpus hit is rarity rather than doubt. The underlying defect is quantitative and provable from the card's own English: fact_en says tephra extends "tens of kilometers" and the Cebuano says "napulo ka mga kilometro" = ten kilometers, an order-of-magnitude understatement of the top of the range (and "ka mga" is ungrammatical after a numeral ligature, which is why I dropped mga to match the attested construction). Worth flagging upstream: this is a systematic MT flattening across the corpus, not a one-off, so other "tens of" cards are likely wrong the same way. emphasis_bis span "tephra" is preserved verbatim.
claims.evidence: binisaya.com/cebuano/tinagpulo: defined — "tenner (n.) — the cardinal number 10". binisaya.com/cebuano/tinagsa: "respective (adj.); one at a time (adv.)" — confirming the tinag- distributive series; binisaya parses tagpulo as tag- + pulo ("ten"), and Wikipedia's Cebuano numerals notes distributives are formed with the tag- prefix (tagpito "seven of each", tag-upat "four of each"). Corpus attests it for precisely this English: ffct-39675 "kalit nga lukso nga tinagpulo ka centimeters" (EN "a sudden jump of tens of centimeters"). The flattening pattern I want on record: dcard-04887 "napulo ka libo ka tuig" for EN "tens of thousands of years"; ffct-32789 "napulo ka milyon nga fungi" for EN "tens of millions of fungi" — so the old wording follows a corpus-wide error rather than defending itself.

claims.new_fact_bis: Kadaghanan sa mga PGAL molecules gamiton aron ma-regenerate ang RuDP, ang sinugdanan nga molecule, aron magpadayon ang pagtuyok sa Calvin cycle ug makakabit pa ug mas daghang carbon dioxide.
claims.reason: Another attestation-bucket close. The defect is a classic false-friend on the English word "fix": fact_en means chemical fixation of CO2, and the Cebuano rendered it with ayo = to repair/heal, so the child reads "the Calvin cycle can heal more carbon dioxide" — a false belief about what fixation is. kabit is dictionary-verified as attach/hook on, and the corpus's own carbon-fixation cards use exactly that root for the same reaction, so makakabit's single body attestation is rarity, not risk. emphasis_bis span "RuDP" is preserved verbatim.
claims.evidence: binisaya.com/cebuano/kabit: verb senses "hang on (to attach or append something)", "hitch (to hook or fasten)", "hook up (to connect or link)", "fix to; attach". Corpus carbon-fixation cards use kabit for this precise reaction: dcard-07990 "ang carbon dioxide sa hangin ikabit sa usa ka five-carbon molecule nga gitawag RuDP" (EN "carbon dioxide from the air is attached to a five-carbon molecule called RuDP") and dcard-03363 (EN "captured and attached to"). makakabit = 1 body, dcard-04146 "ang carbon nga adunay double bond makakabit lamang sa duha ka laing grupo" (EN "a carbon with a double bond can attach to only two other groups") — same chemical-attachment sense as here. Also ffct-30493 "kabiton ang habog nga mga aparador ... sa bungbong" (EN "fasten tall cabinets to the wall").

claims.new_fact_bis:
Nganong makatakod ang paghuy-ab?

Sagad ta mohuy-ab kung makita nato nga naghuy-ab ang lain, mao nga morag mikaylap kini gikan sa usa ka tawo ngadto sa lain.
claims.reason: A confirmed defect, and the hold resolves in favour of a DIFFERENT word than the one proposed. haya is not yawn — it is laying a corpse in state for a wake — so the card currently asks "why is lying-in-state contagious?" and answers that we lie in state when we see others do it. The earlier proposal reached for hikab, which is why the gate flagged thin attestation; but binisaya has no hikab entry at all, whereas huy-ab is a full dictionary entry glossed as yawn and is the better-attested corpus word (5 bodies vs 3), including a card whose sentence is almost identical to this one. So I repaired with huy-ab rather than hikab. Only the three yawn tokens changed; emphasis_bis is empty. Two things to queue elsewhere, not fixed here: this card's fact_en question is in Tagalog ("Bakit nakakahawa ang paghikab?"), an English-side defect; and ffct-03742 carries the identical haya-for-yawn defect and should get the same repair.
claims.evidence: binisaya.com/cebuano/huy-ab: "an involuntary intake of breath through a wide open mouth; usually triggered by fatigue or boredom"; "utter a yawn, as from lack of oxygen or when one is tired"; synonym lingabngab. binisaya.com/cebuano/hikab: "No results found for the Cebuano word hikab" (only suggestions hagabhab, hikap, hukab). Corpus, all 12 cards whose English mentions yawning: huy-ab in 5 bodies — ffct-13918 "Ang paghuy-ab 'makatakod' — kung makita nimo nga mohuy-ab ang uban, lagmit mohuy-ab pud ka!", ffct-10409 "Nganong mohuy-ab man kita?", ffct-07371, ffct-05231, ffct-00757; hikab in 3 — ffct-01993, ffct-07040, ffct-09959; haya in only 2 — this card and ffct-03742 "Ang paghaya usa ka lalom nga pagginhawa". ceb_usage.py --bis haya reports 314 bodies but that is a prefix-match artifact: those hits are hayag/kahayag ("bright", "light"), e.g. ffct-00483 "photosynthesis nagkinahanglan og kahayag" — haya in the yawn sense is unsourced.

claims.new_fact_bis:
Nganong mosaba ang tiyan kon gutom?

Kon walay sulod ang tiyan, mopagawas kini og kemikal nga magsulti sa utok nga oras na para mokaon — mao nga mosaba ang tiyan ug maghunahuna ta og pagkaon!
claims.reason: Real defect, provable from the English: EN is 'your tummy rumbles' but BIS says 'magkalibang ang tiyan' = the stomach defecates / has diarrhea. A child reads a health falsehood (hunger causes diarrhea), not a rumble. The repair word is dictionary-verified, so 2 corpus hits is not evidence against it — and one of those 2 hits is the identical collocation in a sibling card.

claims.new_fact_bis:
Nganong moutot ta?

Moutot ta kay ang mabuot nga bakterya sa atong tinai magbungkag sa pipila ka pagkaon ug maghimo og gas; kon matigom na kini, ipagawas sa lawas — normal ug himsog ra kini.
claims.reason: This is a confirmed false-belief defect, provable from the card's own English. fact_en asks 'Bakit tayo umuutot? / We pass gas...' and the Cebuano asks and answers 'Nganong mokutkot ta? / Mokutkot ta kay...' -- kutkot means to gnaw or scratch. A child reading only the Cebuano is told that gut bacteria making gas is why we GNAW, which is nonsense, and never learns the actual fact. The first agent held it purely on attestation grounds (utot has 0 corpus bodies), and that hold is exactly the case the dictionary is supposed to break: this corpus is itself machine-translated, so its silence is not evidence. Wolff settles both the word and the inflection, giving 'muutut (mangutut)' in a worked example. I take Wolff's muutut in the corpus's own mo-/-o- orthography, which is how this project already spells every mo- + vowel-initial verb, giving moutot. The edit is the minimal one: the prefix, the clause frame and every other word are untouched, and emphasis_bis is empty so no span is at risk. I deliberately did NOT touch 'mabuot nga bakterya' -- it is a corpus singleton where the corpus's own word is 'maayong bakterya' (10 cards), but 'kind bacteria' still delivers 'good bacteria' and is not a false belief, so it falls outside the change-only-what-is-wrong rule.
claims.evidence: Wolff, 'A Dictionary of Cebuano Visayan' (Gutenberg text 40074, headword line): 'utut n fart, gas released from the stomach. ... v [A2N; c] break wind. Muutut (mangutut) ka man lang bisag naay mga tawu! Why do you break wind in front of people! (<-) v [A13P] break wind frequently.' Wolff uses the word in two further entries: 'Nangutut man gud ka! I couldn't help laughing. You broke wind!' (s.v. ahat) and 'Ang bahu sa iyang utut makatublig bunug' (s.v. tubli). binisaya.com/cebuano/utot: '[u.tut.] Noun (act): breaking wind, fart, farting, flatus, wind ... Verb (body): break wind, fart -- to expel intestinal gases through the anus'; binisaya.com/cebuano/pangutot lists 'utot' as the root. Corpus, against: --bis kutkot = 1 body, ffct-04007 'ilang kutkoton ang pagkaon' / EN 'they gnaw on food' -- the gnaw sense, not gas. --en 'pass gas' returns only this card. --bis utot/utut/mangutot/moutot/pangutot = 0 bodies each. The 'otot = muscle' counter-example cited in the hold note no longer exists in the pool: ffct-05580 now reads 'ang kaunuran nga mopataas sa kanto sa atong baba', so 'otot' has 0 bodies and no competing sense. Orthography check for mo- + vowel-initial root: --bis moabot 720 bodies, mouswag 6, mouli 1, all unhyphenated.

claims.reason: fact_en: 'Vision looks blurry when light doesn't land exactly on the retina but falls in front of it or behind it instead.' fact_bis: 'Mahimong hanap ang panan-aw kung ang kahayag dili mahulog sa retina kondili sa atubangan o luyo niini.' Every piece transfers -- hanap = blurry, panan-aw = vision, kahayag dili mahulog sa retina = light doesn't land on the retina, atubangan o luyo = in front of or behind. The optical claim (the retina is the reference plane and the light lands off it on either side) is exactly the English claim, so no false belief is possible. 'hanap' is not a rare or doubtful choice: it is the corpus's own blurry-vision word, used in sibling eye cards. The defect flagged upstream lives entirely in title_bis 'Bulong Retina Focus', which is out of scope here.

claims.reason: The Cebuano contains nothing false: 'Ang dikya mokaon og gagmay nga mga mananap sa dagat sama sa plankton ug gagmay nga isda' is a true and complete sentence matching the first half of fact_en, with the emphasis span 'plankton' intact. What it lacks is the English's trailing clause 'catching them with their trailing tentacles'. I checked the full card record rather than trusting the hold note, and the Tagalog is identically truncated -- fact.tl ends at 'tulad ng plankton at maliliit na isda' with no tentacle clause either. So this is a source-side content gap shared by tl and bis, not a Cebuano-language defect, and repairing only bis would make the Cebuano say more than the Tagalog. An omission also is not a false belief: a child learns what jellyfish eat, just not how they catch it. Route the missing clause to a content pass that fixes tl and bis together; the language hold can close.

claims.reason: fact_en: 'A common cold usually goes away on its own in about seven days, even without medicine.' fact_bis: 'Ang sagad nga sip-on kasagaran maayo ra sa iyang kaugalingon sulod sa pito ka adlaw bisan walay tambal.' All four elements land -- sagad nga sip-on = common cold, kasagaran = usually, sulod sa pito ka adlaw = within seven days, bisan walay tambal = even without medicine. The only construction I doubted was 'maayo ra sa iyang kaugalingon' for 'goes away on its own', since 'maayo' predicated of the illness rather than the person reads oddly to a non-native ear. The corpus settles it: an independent sibling card renders the identical English idiom the identical way, so this is the corpus's established phrasing for self-limiting illness, not a one-off calque in this card. No false belief. title_bis 'Ubo Gikan sa Pito ka Adlaw' swaps cough for cold and drops the clearing-up verb, but that is title-only.
